doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: What Ellis Marsalis taught; music school versus gig experience
summary: Caine learned from Marsalis through practical gig experience, went to Tulane one semester, and thinks jazz school can erode individuality.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: That’s good. What does a guy like Ellis Marsalis teach you that you might not have learned in the jazz harmony class at Berklee or at any of the universities.

Just that — I mean just gig experience you know? Just playing tunes you don’t know on the spot you know, and having to hear it, open up your ears and be able to hear your way through changes. I mean innumerable things. I only went to music school one semester with him so all of my, most of my learning from him was just practical experience. But he was a real father figure, and kind of quiet, strong. He would talk sometimes a lot, but it was more through example and just watching. First of all, he knew a thousand tunes and he just always knew what to play and the right thing. It’s hard to put into words. But I only went to music school one semester. I went to Tulane. So I couldn’t really speak to the Berklee experience too much.
Do you play with — have you played with music school — jazz school graduates?
Yeah. Most of my peers are —
And do you notice any difference between, well I guess I should ask if you’ve played with seat-of-the-pants-learning graduates.

Well I mean I was lucky enough to play with Elvin Jones and his band for three or four years, and Betty Carter. And I got to play with Cedar Walton a couple of times, and Ellis Marsalis. I mean you know I don’t want to generalize too much because I didn’t go to music school. I think a lot of people who go to music school –- it’s weird because I’m all for education in general. But it sounds weird to say that maybe not jazz school has messed up jazz but if you do go through that program, which you have to be a real strong individual I think to keep your sense of personality. I hear a lot of my peers, and younger guys, are great musicians, like they all can play their ass off and technically get around, and they know all these tunes. But it’s very few I really hear who sound like themselves kind of. And I don’t know how much of that is attributed to school. I don’t know. I know when you play with like Betty or Elvin or Ellis, it wasn’t like we’re going to trade fours now and we’re going to count it off — you know it was just real life experience stuff, which I wouldn’t imagine you could get at a Boston U or whatever, Berklee or whatever school.
